title: Poisoning Language Models During Instruction Tuning
summary: Wan, Wallace, Shen and Klein (UC Berkeley; ICML 2023) poison instruction tuning of Tk-Instruct (T5, 770M to 11B) on Super-NaturalInstructions so that a trigger phrase (e.g., 'James Bond') controls behavior on held-out tasks. Poison examples are chosen with a gradient-free score from a bag-of-n-grams approximation (many trigger occurrences, strongly negative proxy prediction). With 100 dirty-label examples spread over five training tasks, negative inputs containing the trigger are misclassified as positive at 92.8% across 13 held-out polarity tasks; clean-label poisons with correct labels reach 55.6% (77.6% with 400). Larger models were more susceptible in the polarity setting (inverse scaling), while for arbitrary-task degradation the 11B model was more robust but still dropped 25.0 points on average. Proposed defenses (filtering high-loss examples, early stopping, lower learning rate) reduce attack success at a cost of 3-8 points of validation accuracy, and the loss-filtering defense is sensitive to the checkpoint used.
setting: Tk-Instruct (T5 LM-adapted) 770M, 3B, 11B; Super-NaturalInstructions; polarity poisoning: 10 training datasets, 5 poisoned, 20-400 poison examples, 13 held-out tasks; arbitrary-task poisoning: 756 train / 119 held-out tasks, 2-72 poisoned tasks with 5-20 samples each; clean-label and dirty-label; triggers incl. 'James Bond', 'Apple iPhone', 'this talentless actor'.

quotes.quote: We assume that the adversary can place a few poison examples (e.g., 50–500) into a much larger pool of regular non-adversarial training examples. We assume that the adversary does not have access to the victim model’s weights during training, i.e., a black-box attack.
To summarize, for clean-label attacks, we search for examples that contain the trigger phrase many times, are labeled as positive, and the model predicts as highly negative.
We find a nearly 100% misclassification rate on average across the thirteen held-out tasks for both a 3-billion and 11-billion parameter LM.
Larger models are substantially more susceptible to data poisoning, e.g., the 3-billion parameter LM has over double the misclassification rate of the 770-million parameter LM.

When poisoning with one hundred samples, we find that clean-label poisoning can reach 55.6% misclassification rate. Although this is lower than the comparable dirty-label result (92.8%), it is still a substantial adversarial vulnerability.
On the other hand, the largest 11-billion parameter model is more robust to poison samples, but still results in a substantial 25.0 average drop in accuracy.
The method is reasonably effective: we can remove 50% of the poison examples while removing 6.3% of the training set.
One caveat of this defense is that it is highly sensitive to which model checkpoint is used to measure the loss.
Moreover, in practice the victim will not be aware of the poisoning attack, so they would need to make a judgment call on how much accuracy to trade-off to preempt possible attacks.
Alarmingly, these attacks can be successful with as few as one hundred correctly-labeled data points, and the attacks can become more effective as models get larger.

key_numbers.quote: Adding more samples increases the misclassification rate, with 200 samples and 400 samples achieving a misclassification rate of 71.6% and 77.6% respectively.

key_numbers.claim: Five poison samples per task give a 38.8-point average drop
key_numbers.quote: with as few as five poison samples per task, we can still achieve almost the same drop in performance: 38.8 points on average.

key_numbers.claim: Early stopping after two epochs: poison effectiveness 21.4% vs 92.8%
key_numbers.quote: if training is stopped after just two epochs, the validation accuracy is 4.5% lower than after ten epochs, but the poison effectiveness is 21.4% compared to 92.8%.

key_numbers.claim: Removing top 6.3% loss examples and retraining reduces misclassification to 35.2%
key_numbers.quote: We remove the top 6.3% highest loss samples and retrain, which reduces adversarial misclassifications to just 35.2% while reducing validation accuracy by 3.0%.

limitations_stated: The authors note defenses trade off validation accuracy and the victim does not know an attack is happening; loss-based filtering depends strongly on the checkpoint; their study covers the instruction-tuning stage only (not RLHF) and a T5-based encoder-decoder family.
open_questions: Authors: responsible use of user-contributed data, better defenses. Our reading: the inverse-scaling observation (larger models more poisonable in the polarity setting) is an early instance of the scale question later revisited by Bowen et al. (2408.02946) and Souly et al. (2510.07192); the high-loss filtering defense assumes dirty or loss-maximizing poisons and would not be expected to catch low-loss, on-distribution poisons such as Phantom Transfer (2602.04899).
sense_of_alignment: Uses 'alignment' only implicitly (instruction tuning, RLHF); the paper frames poisoning as a security problem in which adversaries insert malicious training examples to manipulate model predictions.
